---
title: Core concepts
description: "The model behind the arkitekt Python library: apps, actions, implementations, agents, tasks, ports and structures, injection, state, lifecycle hooks, streaming, workflows and disconnect policies. Each concept comes with a minimal example."
---

This page introduces the vocabulary you need to read the rest of the Python guide. Each concept has
a platform-wide definition in the [terminology](/docs/design/terminology) section. Here you see what
it looks like in code, and how the concepts fit together at runtime.

## The big picture

```text
 your code                         the platform                         somebody else
┌──────────────────┐   run(app)   ┌──────────────────────────┐  call   ┌──────────────┐
│ App              │ ───────────► │ Rekuest                  │ ◄────── │ Orkestrator, │
│  @app.action f   │  registers   │  action  "f"             │         │ a script, a  │
│  @app.workflow w │  implement-  │  implementation of "f"   │  task   │ workflow …   │
│  @app.state S    │  ations      │    by this app, for you  │ ──────► │              │
└──────────────────┘              │  agent  (this process)   │         └──────────────┘
          ▲                       └────────────┬─────────────┘
          │        task: run f(x=1)            │
          └────────────────────────────────────┘
```

1. You **declare** an `App` and decorate functions. Nothing connects yet.
2. `run(app)` authenticates, starts an **agent** for this process and registers one
   **implementation** per decorated function with [Rekuest](/docs/build/concepts/services/rekuest). The
   implementation is attached to an **action**, the abstract "what", identified by the function's
   inputs and outputs.
3. Someone calls the action. Rekuest creates a **task** and routes it to an agent that implements
   the action.
4. Your agent receives the task, turns the arguments into Python objects, calls your function and
   reports progress, logs, yields and the result back.

## App

An `App` is a **declaration**: who the app is and what it offers. Declaring it does no I/O.

```python
from arkitekt import App

app = App(
    "com.example.nuclei",   # identifier: defaults to the file name
    "0.2.0",                # version: semver
    description="Nucleus segmentation for widefield images",
    services=[],            # service clients the actions use, see below
)
```

The identifier and version tell the platform which app an implementation belongs to. Together they
make up the app's [manifest](/docs/build/reference/manifest). There is no manifest *file*: the
manifest is computed from the declaration (`app.manifest`), and `arkitekt inspect all` prints what
the app would register without connecting.

An app is declared once, at module level, in a file the CLI can import. By default it is a variable
called `app` in `app.py` (see [Your first app](/docs/build/tutorials/python-first-app)).

## Action and implementation

`@app.action` turns a function into an [implementation](/docs/design/terminology/implementation) of
an [action](/docs/design/terminology/action):

```python
from typing import Annotated
from arkitekt import App, Description, run

app = App("hello", "0.1.0")


@app.action
def greet(
    name: Annotated[str, Description("Who to greet")] = "world",
    times: Annotated[int, Description("How often to say it")] = 1,
) -> str:
    """Greet

    Says hello, possibly several times.
    """
    return " ".join([f"Hello {name}!"] * times)
```

- The **parameters** become the action's input [ports](/docs/design/terminology/port) and the
  **return annotation** its output ports. A tuple return gives several outputs. Type hints are
  required: they drive validation, the generated form in Orkestrator and how values are serialized.
- The **first line of the docstring** is the action's title, and the rest is its description.
  `{{name}}` placeholders in the description are filled with the call's arguments in the UI.
- `Annotated[..., Description(...)]` documents a single port. `Default`, `Units`, `Requires` and
  `Provides` are further markers you can add the same way.
- A default value makes the port optional, and `Optional[...]` makes it nullable.

The **action** is the abstract "what", defined by its ports. It is what users search for and what
workflows are built from. The **implementation** is the concrete "how": this function, in this
app, at this version, running for this user. Two apps can implement the same action, and the
platform picks an implementation when a task is created.

The decorated function stays an ordinary function. You can call it directly in tests. If it takes
a `task`, pass `Task.local()`, a stand-in that logs to the console:

```python
from arkitekt import Task

assert measure_nuclei(min_size=10, task=Task.local()).count > 0
```

`@app.action` takes keyword options when used with parentheses. The ones you will use most:

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name=` | Override the action's name (defaults to the function name) |
| `effects=` | What running it again would do to the world: [`Effects`](/docs/build/guides/python/durable-execution#effects) |
| `policy=` | What happens to a running task if this agent loses its connection: [disconnect policy](#disconnect-policy) |
| `concurrency=` | `"serial"` (default) or `"parallel"`: whether this agent runs several tasks of this action at once |
| `locks=` | Named locks a task must hold while it runs. Tasks that need the same lock wait for each other |
| `widgets=`, `port_groups=`, `validators=` | Per-port UI widgets, grouping and validation |

## Agent

An **agent** is one running process that serves implementations: your `run(app)`, or a container
started from your plugin. It holds a websocket to Rekuest, receives tasks, runs them and reports back.
When you restart the process, a new agent session starts under the same agent name. That continuity
is what lets the platform [resume workflows](/docs/build/guides/python/durable-execution) after a crash.

You rarely touch the agent directly. It matters because it defines what "the agent died" means: the
process exited, crashed, lost power or stayed disconnected past the grace window.

## Task

A [task](/docs/design/terminology/task) is **one run of an action**. It has an id, belongs to the
user and organization who started it, can be cancelled, and records everything that happened in its
event history.

Inside your function the running task is available by annotating a parameter with `Task`. That
parameter is **injected**. It is not a port, and callers never see it:

```python
from arkitekt import App, Task

app = App("measure", "0.1.0")


@app.action
def measure(count: int, *, task: Task) -> float:
    """Measure"""
    total = 0.0
    for i in range(count):
        task.progress(int(100 * i / count), f"sample {i}")
        total += read_sensor()
    task.log(f"read {count} samples")
    return total / count
```

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `task.log(message, level)` | A log line attached to the task, visible in the UI |
| `task.progress(percent, message)` | Progress, shown live |
| `task.pausepoint()` | A point where the task pauses if someone paused it |
| `task.now()`, `task.random()`, `task.sleep()`, `task.record(fn)` | Values taken from outside, **recorded** so a resumed workflow gets the same ones back ([durable execution](/docs/build/guides/python/durable-execution)) |
| `task.retry(...)`, `task.hold(...)`, `task.guard(...)` | Deciding about a lost step in a workflow |
| `task.id`, `task.user`, `task.org` | Who and what this task is |

Every method has an `a`-prefixed async twin (`await task.aprogress(...)`) for `async def` actions.
With the `tqdm` extra, `from arkitekt.tqdm import tqdm` gives a progress bar that reports to the task.

## Ports, types and structures

A port may only name a type the app knows how to transport:

| Kind | Examples | Travels as |
|---|---|---|
| Scalars | `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `Enum` subclasses | the value |
| Containers | `list[...]`, `dict[str, ...]`, `Optional[...]`, `Union[...]`, tuples as multiple returns | the value |
| **Models** | a class decorated with `@app.model` | the value, field by field |
| **Service structures** | `Volume`, `SingleChannelImage`, `LabelMask` from `mikro.arkitekt.specs` | a reference: the id of an object stored in the service |
| **Registered structures** | your own class, via `app.register_structure(...)` | a reference that your expander resolves |
| **Memory structures** | e.g. `np.ndarray`, via `app.memory_structure(...)` | a reference to an object kept on this agent |

This is the *pass-by-reference* model. Large data never travels between apps inline. It lives in a
data service like [Mikro](/docs/build/concepts/services/mikro) and only its id travels. The receiving app
fetches it again ("expands" it). [Types & data](/docs/build/guides/python/types) explains each kind
in detail. The platform-wide concept is described under [structure](/docs/design/terminology/structure).

Using a type the app does not know is an error when the app is declared, not when it is called.

## Injection by annotation

Several kinds of parameters are filled in by the runtime rather than by the caller. Arkitekt tells
them apart by their **type annotation**:

| Annotated with | Injected value |
|---|---|
| `Task` | The running task |
| A service client (`Mikro`, `Fluss`, …) | A connected client, if the service is listed in `App(services=[...])` |
| An `@app.state` class | The app's live state instance |
| An `@app.context` class | The shared context built by a startup hook |
| The class passed as `App(app_context=...)` | The value passed to `run(app, context=...)` |
| An `@app.declare` protocol | A proxy that calls another app's actions (workflows only) |

Everything else is a port. Injected parameters can go anywhere in the signature. Making them
keyword-only (after `*`) is a readable convention.

## Services

Actions that need a platform service name it in `services=` and take its client by annotation:

```python
from arkitekt import App, Task
from mikro import Mikro, mikro_service
from mikro.arkitekt.specs import Volume

app = App("inspect-volume", "0.1.0", services=[mikro_service])


@app.action
def describe(volume: Volume, mikro: Mikro, task: Task) -> str:
    """Describe Volume"""
    task.progress(50, "Reading")
    return f"{volume.data.shape}"
```

Listing a service does two things. It declares a **requirement**, which the user approves when the
app first connects, and it makes the service's structures (here `Volume`) usable as ports. Pass the
service object (`mikro_service`), not the client class. Passing a class raises `TypeError`.

## State, context and lifecycle

Some things live longer than one task: a connection to a device, a loaded model, the position of a
stage. Arkitekt has three declarations for them, all populated by **startup hooks**:

| Declaration | For | Visible to others? |
|---|---|---|
| `@app.state` | Values others should see change live: a stage position, a queue length | Yes, published to the platform and patched as it changes |
| `@app.context` | Heavy or private objects: a model, a device handle | No |
| `App(app_context=Setup)` | Configuration of this installation, given to `run(app, context=...)` | No |

`@app.startup`, `@app.shutdown` and `@app.background` run when the agent starts providing, stops,
or for as long as it runs. The details and a full device example are in
[State & lifecycle](/docs/build/guides/python/state-lifecycle).

## Streaming

An action written as a **generator** streams. Each `yield` is delivered to the caller as it happens,
and a workflow can process items while later ones are still being produced:

```python
from typing import Generator
from arkitekt import App

app = App("counter", "0.1.0")


@app.action
def count_to(n: int) -> Generator[int, None, None]:
    """Count To"""
    for i in range(n):
        yield i
```

Async generators (`AsyncGenerator[...]`) work the same way. Streaming is what makes
[real-time workflows](/docs/design/philosophy/realtime) possible.

## Calling other actions: workflows

A plain action **may not call other actions**. An action that orchestrates others is declared with
`@app.workflow` instead. It names what it needs from another app as a **protocol**:

```python
from typing import Protocol
from arkitekt import App, Task

app = App("pipeline", "0.1.0")


@app.declare(app="segmentation", auto_resolvable=True, min=1)
class Segmentation(Protocol):
    def count_cells(self, image_id: str) -> int:
        """Count Cells"""
        ...


@app.workflow
def count_twice(segmentation: Segmentation, image_id: str, *, task: Task) -> int:
    """Count Twice"""
    first = segmentation.count_cells(image_id)
    second = segmentation.count_cells(image_id)
    return max(first, second)
```

The restriction exists because only a workflow can be **resumed** if its agent dies. A plain action
that had called three others and then crashed would have no way to find those calls again.
[Workflows](/docs/build/guides/python/workflows) covers protocols and calling. [Durable execution](/docs/build/guides/python/durable-execution)
covers what happens on failure.

## Execution and effects

Every implementation carries two claims that decide what happens when an agent dies mid-task:

- **Execution**: `PLAIN` (`@app.action`) or `WORKFLOW` (`@app.workflow`). A plain task whose agent
  dies ends **LOST** and the caller decides what to do. A workflow whose agent dies is **resumed**.
- **Effects**: what running it again would do to the world. The values are `NONE`, `REPEATABLE`,
  `UNKNOWN` (the default) and `IRREVERSIBLE`. This claim is information for whoever decides after a
  loss. It is never a rule the platform acts on.

```python
from arkitekt import App, Effects

app = App("liquid-handler", "0.1.0", effects=Effects.IRREVERSIBLE)  # default for this app


@app.action(effects=Effects.NONE)   # this one only reads
def read_absorbance(well: str) -> float:
    """Read Absorbance"""
    ...
```

See [Durable execution](/docs/build/guides/python/durable-execution) and the design page
[Durable execution](/docs/build/concepts/durable-execution) for the full model.

## Disconnect policy [#disconnect-policy]

Separate from an agent *dying* is an agent temporarily *losing its connection*. By default a
running task keeps going and reports when the link returns. That is right for a six-hour
acquisition. For an action whose safety depends on being stoppable ("move the stage until I say
stop"), declare that losing the link is itself a stop condition:

```python
from arkitekt import App, CancelOnDisconnect

app = App("stage", "0.1.0")


@app.action(policy=CancelOnDisconnect(grace=2.0))
async def jog(direction: str) -> None:
    """Jog

    Moves until cancelled. Stops if control is lost for more than two seconds.
    """
    ...
```

The policy is enforced inside your process, because the server cannot reach a disconnected agent.
An `async` action is cancelled at its next `await`. A **sync** action runs in a worker thread,
which cannot be killed. It stops only at a `koil.check_cancelled()` call, so long-running sync loops
must poll it. This narrows the window in which hardware keeps running after control is lost. It is
not a safety interlock, and hardware that must stop needs its own watchdog.

## Sync or async?

Both are supported, for actions, hooks and workflows. Use `async def` when your code awaits I/O or
calls async clients (`await mikro.acreate_folder(...)`), and plain `def` for CPU-bound or blocking
library code. Sync functions run in a worker thread, so they don't block the agent. Every client and
task method exists in both forms: `x(...)` and `await ax(...)`.
